notable_claims: An individual attempted to use university system administrators to censor or terminate a professor's network access due to personal disagreements in a public forum.
classification.summary: Marie Coffin, a mathematics professor at Clemson University, announced her departure from the rec.arts.poems newsgroup. This decision followed an attempt by Barbara Taylor of cas.org to have Coffin's university account revoked by complaining to the system administrator about their interpersonal disputes.
classification.title: An open letter to rap / Marie Coffin

notable_claims: A user attempted to have another user's university account 'yanked' by complaining to the system administrator about newsgroup behavior.
The author claims this was an attempt to silence her through threats and intimidation.
classification.summary: Marie Coffin announces her departure from the rec.arts.poems newsgroup after another user, Barbara, contacted Coffin's university system administrator to request that her account be terminated. Coffin describes this as an attempt at silencing and intimidation through the use of institutional authority. She notes that while her department did not pressure her to leave, she chose to do so to avoid further embarrassment to her colleagues.
classification.title: An open letter to rap / Marie Coffin

notable_claims: A university postmaster disabled a user account based on complaints from external newsgroup 'trollers'.
classification.summary: A student at the University of Utah reported that their email account was summarily disabled by a postmaster following complaints from users of the alt.religion.kibology newsgroup. The account was reinstated after the student appealed to the postmaster's supervisor.
classification.title: I was censored by kibologists

notable_claims: The user's university account was suspended following complaints from other Usenet users.
Account reinstatement was achieved by appealing to the postmaster's superior.
classification.summary: Roger Bryner reports that his University of Utah account was temporarily suspended after he posted informational messages in response to 'trolls' from the alt.religion.kibology newsgroup. The suspension occurred after a small group of users complained to the university postmaster. Bryner successfully had his account reinstated by contacting the postmaster's superior and expressed intent to pursue further legal or administrative action.
classification.title: I was censored by kibologists

notable_claims: A student lost university network access due to a post made from their account without their consent.
classification.summary: A student at the University of Missouri-Rolla reported losing their network access for the remainder of the semester. The disciplinary action followed a hate speech post titled "vietnamese suck" that was sent from the student's account without their knowledge.
classification.title: [soc.culture.vietnamese] Re: ****READ ME****

notable_claims: Forging posts and email on the Internet is relatively easy
University administration may penalize users for forged content attributed to their accounts
classification.summary: Joe Miller discusses the consequences of a forged post attributed to him on the Internet. Barry Kitson advises that such forgeries are common and authenticity cannot be guaranteed online. As a result of the incident, Miller expects to lose his network access for the remainder of the semester.
classification.title: Re: ****READ ME****

notable_claims: The student's account was lost due to faculty complaints about offensive posts
The university maintained a policy against posting offensive material, which the student claimed was subjectively applied
classification.summary: A student at the University of Missouri discusses the loss of their network account following complaints from faculty members regarding offensive material. The student argues that they did not post the content in question and critiques the subjective nature of the university's policy on offensive material.
classification.title: [soc.culture.vietnamese] Re: ****READ ME****

notable_claims: Faculty members complained about the user's expressed views
The institution has a policy against posting offensive material
The definition of 'offensive' is subjective based on the reader
classification.summary: A student named Joe describes facing disciplinary pressure and potential loss of computer access due to posting material deemed 'offensive' by faculty. He expresses frustration with the subjective nature of the institution's policy on offensive content. The exchange highlights the tension between university acceptable use policies and individual expression.
classification.title: Re: ****READ ME****

classification.summary: A reposted message addressing a University of Utah student who claimed to be censored. The author argues that the student's repetitive posting of boilerplate messages constituted offensive behavior rather than legitimate communication.
classification.title: Re: I was censored by kibologists

notable_claims: Steve Wolff stated that the concept of an 'attractive nuisance' does not apply to the NSF AUP.
classification.summary: The post discusses whether hosting commercial information accessible via NSFNet constitutes a violation of the National Science Foundation's Acceptable Use Policy (AUP). It references a statement by Steve Wolff regarding the 'attractive nuisance' doctrine in relation to the AUP.
classification.title: AUP's and WWW commercial sites

identity.subject: [comp.infosystems.www]  Re: AUP's and WWW commercial sites

notable_claims: The NSF AUP does not prohibit commercial entities from hosting WWW servers or accepting email orders.
Responsibility for AUP compliance rests with the user accessing the data, not the provider.
DOE/FermiLab policies could serve as an 'escape hatch' for acceptable use on NSFNET.
classification.summary: The author discusses the interpretation of the National Science Foundation (NSF) Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) regarding commercial content on the World Wide Web. He argues that hosting commercial information is not an AUP violation; rather, the responsibility lies with the user to ensure their access complies with policy. The post suggests that the NSF AUP was becoming obsolete as the internet transitioned toward commercialization.
classification.title: Re: AUP's and WWW commercial sites

notable_claims: ACNS improperly claimed authority to judge offenses and impose summary punishments on students
The ACNS due-process policy contradicted explicit University policy
classification.summary: This post critiques the computing policies of Northwestern University's Academic Computing and Network Services (ACNS). While praising the intellectual freedom policy, it argues that the due-process policy is fatally flawed because ACNS claims authority to impose summary punishments on students. The author suggests this contradicts broader university policy regarding student voice and academic freedom.
classification.title: Re: Northwestern U. computer policies

notable_claims: ACNS policies on summary suspension of network access contradicted official university disciplinary procedures.
The ACNS guidelines regarding the distribution of programs were viewed as overly broad and potentially violating free expression.
University policy required student participation in the formation of policies affecting them, which was questioned regarding ACNS.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides a detailed critique of the computing policies at Northwestern University's Academic Computing and Network Services (ACNS). He argues that ACNS improperly claimed authority to impose summary punishments on students, bypassing established university due process and disciplinary procedures. The critique also addresses concerns regarding vague privacy language, contradictions in security loophole reporting, and overly broad restrictions on software sharing.
classification.title: Re: Northwestern U. computer policies

notable_claims: Comparing university email to official letterhead injures academic freedom.
Treating email as institutional letterhead increases the likelihood of university liability for faculty and student messages.
classification.summary: The post argues against the comparison of university email usage to the use of official university paper letterhead. It claims that treating email as official institutional communication harms academic freedom and increases the institution's legal liability for user content.
classification.title: Is E-mail letterhead?

notable_claims: Treating university email as official letterhead injures academic freedom.
Institutional control or prior review of student publications/communications may actually increase a school's legal liability for libel.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to a query regarding whether university email constitutes official 'letterhead,' which some administrators used as a justification to restrict private correspondence. Kadie argues that treating email as letterhead harms academic freedom and potentially increases institutional liability. He supports his position by citing student codes, the Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students, and legal precedents regarding student press.
classification.title: Re: Is E-mail letterhead?

notable_claims: Iowa State University allegedly violated written due process policies and federal student privacy laws in response to a user's policy violation.
classification.summary: A repost from the Electronic Frontier Foundation regarding Iowa State University's handling of a user's policy violation. The post alleges that the university violated its own due process policies, federal student privacy laws, and constitutional protections in its response.
classification.title: Postings by Andrzej Janus (ajanus@iastate.edu)

notable_claims: The public announcement of a student's computer account suspension may violate FERPA.
Rapid suspension of network access without formal hearings may contradict university due process policies.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques Iowa State University's suspension of a student for using university resources to conduct for-profit activities on Usenet. Kadie argues that the rapid suspension and public announcement may have violated the university's own due process policies, constitutional protections, and the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA).
classification.title: Re: Postings by Andrzej Janus (ajanus@iastate.edu)

Technical delays and disk space limitations on servers like munnari contributed to the loss of binary news articles.
classification.summary: Robert Elz reports that the University of Melbourne has decided to stop carrying Usenet newsgroups related to adult content (alt.sex and alt.binaries.pictures.erotica). He attributes previous delivery failures to technical bottlenecks at munnari and ANU servers, but confirms a new institutional policy to ban these groups. He directs complaints regarding this censorship to the University's Vice Chancellor.
